title_en: Rebuilding of the Kaabah and the Black Stone Arbitration
title_ar: إعادة بناء الكعبة المشرفة وتحكيم وضع الحجر الأسود
summary: When the Quraysh rebuilt the Kaabah after it was damaged by floods and fire, a dispute arose over which tribe would have the honour of placing the Black Stone. Muhammad ﷺ, before his prophethood, resolved the crisis with wisdom by having all tribal leaders hold a cloth and lift the stone together.
narrative:
Around 605 CE, approximately five years before the beginning of the Prophethood, the Kaabah in Makkah was damaged by a severe flood that weakened its walls, and a subsequent fire that caused further deterioration. The Quraysh decided to demolish and rebuild the structure with better foundations. Ibn Hisham records that the Quraysh were initially reluctant to tear down the sacred building, fearing divine punishment, until a man named al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah struck the wall with his pickaxe and suffered no harm — which the Quraysh took as a sign that they could proceed.

The tribes of Quraysh divided the reconstruction among themselves, with each tribe responsible for a section of the building. Ibn Hisham records that they used stone quarried from the surrounding mountains, as well as timber salvaged from a Byzantine ship that had been wrecked near Jeddah. A Coptic craftsman named Baqum is mentioned in the sources as having contributed skills to the construction alongside Qurayshi workers.

When the walls were raised to the height where the Black Stone — al-Hajar al-Aswad — needed to be placed back in its eastern corner, a serious dispute erupted among the clans of Quraysh. Each tribe claimed the honour of placing the sacred stone, and the argument grew so heated that some leaders drew swords and an inter-tribal war seemed imminent. The matter reached an impasse for several days.

Ibn Hisham and al-Tabari both record that an elder among the Quraysh proposed that they accept the judgment of the first person to enter the sanctuary from the Banu Shaybah gate. The first to enter that morning was Muhammad ibn Abdillah ﷺ, then approximately thirty-five years of age and known throughout Makkah as al-Amin — the Trustworthy. When the assembled leaders saw him, they said: 'This is al-Amin — we are pleased with him. This is Muhammad.'

They explained the dispute to him. The Prophet ﷺ asked for a large cloth to be brought. He placed the Black Stone in its centre himself, and then called a representative from each tribe to take hold of the edges of the cloth. Together, all the tribes lifted the stone and raised it to the appropriate height, and the Prophet ﷺ then took the stone with his own hands and set it into its designated place in the corner.

Ibn Kathir in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah notes that this incident demonstrates the high regard in which the Prophet ﷺ was held by his community even before revelation, and the natural wisdom and equanimity that were among the signs of his prophethood to come. The solution was elegant: every tribe participated in the honour, and no blood was shed. The reconstruction of the Kaabah was completed, though the Quraysh — due to insufficient funds from lawful sources — left out a section known as the Hijr Ismail on the north side, which they could not include within the sacred building. The Prophet ﷺ later told Aisha RA that had the Quraysh not been new to Islam, he would have incorporated the Hijr Ismail fully within the Kaabah, as recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari.
hadith_references: Sahih al-Bukhari 1584 — Aisha RA: the Prophet ﷺ on the Hijr Ismail
